pamphlet_excerpts: Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards: There are two types of venomous snakes in the United States (p. 22).
Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards Principle 2: Pit vipers (rattlesnakes, copperheads, and cottonmouths) have triangular heads with pit marks on both sides of the head (p. 22).
Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards Principle 3: Coral snakes have black snouts and bands of red and yellow separated by bands of black (p. 22).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards): A hiking stick does double duty when you walk through places where snakes might lurk (p. 22).
Step 2 (Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards): Walk slowly and use the stick to poke amongst ones and brush ahead (p. 22).
Step 3 (Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards): Watch where you put your hands as you collect firewood or climb over rocks and logs (p. 22).
Step 4 (Winter Sports Safety, First Aid & Hazards): The bite of a nonvenomous snake causes only minor puncture wounds (p. 22).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (10 Scout Basic Essentials): Divide group gear so that each person carries a fair share. 3 (p. 53).
Step 2 (10 Scout Basic Essentials): Gradually replace your heavy equipment and clothing with lighter items (p. 53).
Step 3 (10 Scout Basic Essentials): Choose lightweight hiking boots over stiff, heavy footwear. 5 (p. 53).
Step 4 (10 Scout Basic Essentials): Prepare one-pot meals featuring pasta, powdered sauce mixes, and other ingredients that are dry, easy to pack, and not very heavy. 6 (p. 53).

pamphlet_excerpts: Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics: Extending courtesy to other outdoor visitors is a natural habit of backpackers (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 2: If you carry amobile telephone for emergency communication, turn it off and stow it in your pack until you need (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 3: Appreciate the company of those you meet on the trail and at campsites near yours, but respect their desire for quiet and solitude (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 4: If you encounter horseback riders or pack animals, stop and ask the lead rider (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): The lead rider will probably ask you to step a fewpaces downhill from the trail and stand quietly while the animals pass (p. 61).
Step 2 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If you encounter other hikers or backpackers going uphill when you are going downhill, give them the right of-way (p. 61).
Step 3 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): Step aside on a rock or a log to minimize your impact (p. 61).
Step 4 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If possible, camp away from trails and other visitors (p. 61).

pamphlet_excerpts: Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics: Extending courtesy to other outdoor visitors is a natural habit of backpackers (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 2: If you carry amobile telephone for emergency communication, turn it off and stow it in your pack until you need (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 3: Appreciate the company of those you meet on the trail and at campsites near yours, but respect their desire for quiet and solitude (p. 61).
Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics Principle 4: If you encounter horseback riders or pack animals, stop and ask the lead rider (p. 61).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): The lead rider will probably ask you to step a fewpaces downhill from the trail and stand quietly while the animals pass (p. 61).
Step 2 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If you encounter other hikers or backpackers going uphill when you are going downhill, give them the right of-way (p. 61).
Step 3 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): Step aside on a rock or a log to minimize your impact (p. 61).
Step 4 (Leave No Trace & Outdoor Ethics): If possible, camp away from trails and other visitors (p. 61).
